tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of overdue library books has risen since March.
A number of neighbours was unable to join the street clean-up.
Neither the coach nor the players were copied on the match email.
Each of the flatmates have filed a chore preference form.
There are several typos in the potluck recipe list.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of overdue library books has risen since March.**

The head of this sentence is "the number," which names one count of overdue books, not the books themselves. Singular subjects take singular verbs, so "has risen" is the right match. Mentally swapping in "that total has risen" makes the agreement feel natural.

That agreement is clean — singular "the number" correctly pairs with "has risen."
**B) A number of neighbours was unable to join the street clean-up.**

"A number of neighbours" means several neighbours, so the verb must be plural. The written "was unable" wrongly treats "number" as a singular head. Flip the article test: a number = many people, so the repair is "were unable."

Mark it wrong and prefer "A number of neighbours were unable to join the street clean-up."
**C) Neither the coach nor the players were copied on the match email.**

With neither…nor, agreement follows the nearer subject — the one sitting just before the verb. Here that noun is plural "players," so "were copied" is correct. Ignore "coach" when you choose the verb; proximity, not the first noun, decides.

**Tip:** Cover the first noun and read only from "nor" onward.

Accept the line — nearer plural "players" after nor rightly takes "were copied."
**D) Each of the flatmates have filed a chore preference form.**

"Each of the flatmates" is singular even though "flatmates" looks plural. "Each" picks out one member at a time, and the of-phrase never takes control of the verb. The written "have filed" agrees with the wrong noun.

That agreement fails — rewrite as "Each of the flatmates has filed a chore preference form."
**E) There are several typos in the potluck recipe list.**

The delayed subject after "there" is plural "typos," so "there are" agrees correctly. In there-constructions the real subject follows the verb — match that noun's number. Here several typos make the plural verb unavoidable.

That works: plural "typos" after there correctly calls for "there are."
tasks.solution_overview:
You are judging five everyday sentences for subject-verb agreement. Library books, a street clean-up, a match email, flatmate chores, and a potluck list supply the setting — the verbs are what matter.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set mixes four classic traps: the number of versus a number of, neither…nor proximity, each of, and there is/are. Distracting plurals sit next to the verb on purpose, so your job is to name the true grammatical subject first. Once that subject is clear, the right verb number usually follows without debate.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cross out of-phrases and insert material, then ask whether the leftover head is singular or plural. For neither…nor, check only the noun sitting next to the verb. For there-constructions, look past the verb to the delayed subject and match that.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Every applicant for the baking class receives a starter kit.
The chef, along with two helpers, were present at the tasting.
There is a backlog of laundry waiting for the dryer.
Neither the twins nor their aunt has signed the permission slip.
A number of guests have requested a later checkout.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Every applicant for the baking class receives a starter kit.**

"Every applicant" is grammatically singular even though many people are implied. Singular "receives" is therefore correct with "a starter kit." Words like every and each always pick units one at a time in formal exam English.

This is sound — "every applicant" locks in singular "receives."
**B) The chef, along with two helpers, were present at the tasting.**

"Along with two helpers" is only a parenthetical add-on; the subject remains singular "The chef." Inserts introduced by along with, as well as, or together with never create a compound plural subject. The written "were present" wrongly steals plurality from the helpers.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "The chef, along with two helpers, was present at the tasting."
**C) There is a backlog of laundry waiting for the dryer.**

The delayed subject is singular "a backlog," so "there is" agrees. Do not let the plural idea inside "of laundry" steal the agreement — the head noun is backlog. Once you isolate that head, the singular verb is obvious.

Hold onto this: singular "backlog" after there correctly takes "there is."
**D) Neither the twins nor their aunt has signed the permission slip.**

After neither…nor the nearer subject is singular "aunt," so "has signed" is right. Proximity overrides the plural feel of "twins" at the front of the chain. Read only from "nor" to the verb when you decide number.

**Tip:** Neither…nor: last noun wins.

Call this correct: nearer singular "aunt" after nor takes "has signed."
**E) A number of guests have requested a later checkout.**

"A number of guests" means several guests, so plural "have requested" is correct. Flip the article test if you hesitate: a number = many, the number = one figure. Here the plural verb matches the plural sense cleanly.

The plural reading works: "a number of guests" rightly takes "have requested."
tasks.solution_overview:
Five more agreement checks, this time around a baking class, a tasting, laundry, a permission slip, and a hotel checkout. Same game: decide whether the sentence as written is fine.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch how "every" forces a singular verb, how along with never pluralises the head subject, and how neither…nor still obeys proximity. "A number of" again behaves as a plural group, while there is/are tracks the delayed subject. Parenthetical helpers are especially tempting distractors in this set.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cross out along with / as well as inserts before you judge the verb. For every/each, treat the subject as one person or thing at a time. For neither…nor, check only the nearer noun; for there-lines, name what comes after the verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of complaints have fallen after the repair.
Neither the kitchen nor the bathrooms was cleaned last week.
There is three outstanding photos on the shared album.
Each partner in the dance duo have veto rights over the routine.
The data from the pilot survey support the forecast.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of complaints have fallen after the repair.**

"The number of complaints" is a singular total — one count of complaints after the repair. The written "have fallen" wrongly agrees with plural "complaints" in the of-phrase. Keep focusing on "number" as the true subject head.

Score it false and use "The number of complaints has fallen after the repair."
**B) Neither the kitchen nor the bathrooms was cleaned last week.**

With neither…nor, only the nearer noun controls the verb. Here that noun is plural "bathrooms," so "was cleaned" is the wrong match. Singular "kitchen" at the front is irrelevant once nor has spoken.

That proximity miss fails — prefer "Neither the kitchen nor the bathrooms were cleaned last week."
**C) There is three outstanding photos on the shared album.**

"Three outstanding photos" is plural, so you need "there are," not "there is." Count what follows the verb in there-constructions. The numeral three is an immediate plural cue.

Don't accept that; rewrite as "There are three outstanding photos on the shared album."
**D) Each partner in the dance duo have veto rights over the routine.**

"Each partner" takes a singular verb even when "duo" suggests two people. The written "have veto rights" agrees with the wrong idea of plurality. Strip the of-phrase and hear "each has."

Mark it wrong and prefer "Each partner in the dance duo has veto rights over the routine."
**E) The data from the pilot survey support the forecast.**

In formal usage "data" is treated as plural, so "support" is the agreed verb here. On exam papers, keep that plural default unless the prompt clearly marks informal style. The of-phrase "from the pilot survey" does not change the number.

**Tip:** Formal exam default: data → plural verb.

Trust the verb here: formal plural "data" correctly takes "support."
tasks.solution_overview:
This round is deliberately full of broken agreement: complaints after a repair, cleaning rotas, a shared album, dance partners, and survey data. Four sentences are wrong on purpose; one is clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

You will again meet the number of, neither…nor, there is/are, and each — plus formal plural "data." The traps work by dangling a plural noun next to a singular verb (or the reverse). Spotting which noun actually governs the verb is the whole exercise.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Isolate the real subject — the number, the nearer nor-noun, the post-verbal noun after there, or each — then check whether the written verb matches. For data on formal papers, prefer plural agreement unless the prompt clearly allows informal singular usage.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the referee nor the linesmen were briefed overnight.
The gardener, together with the volunteers, has approved the planting plan.
There are no further objections from the neighbours.
Every parcel above two kilos requires dual labelling.
A number of interns was assigned to the summer festival.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the referee nor the linesmen were briefed overnight.**

The nearer subject after neither…nor is plural "linesmen," so "were briefed" agrees. Cover "referee" and read from "nor" onward if you want a quick check. Proximity, not the first noun, decides the verb.

That pairing is sound — nearer "linesmen" correctly yields plural "were briefed."
**B) The gardener, together with the volunteers, has approved the planting plan.**

"Together with the volunteers" does not pluralise "The gardener"; singular "has approved" is correct. With-phrases are parenthetical, not co-subjects. Strip the insert and the sentence still stands as "the gardener has approved."

Accept the line: singular gardener stays the head with "has approved."
**C) There are no further objections from the neighbours.**

Plural "objections" correctly takes "there are." The word "no" does not change number — you still match the noun that follows. Here further objections are clearly plural.

Leave it as written — plural "objections" correctly take "there are."
**D) Every parcel above two kilos requires dual labelling.**

"Every parcel" is singular, so "requires" is right. Every and each plus a singular noun lock in a singular verb even when many parcels are implied. Dual labelling does not affect agreement.

Solid agreement here: "every parcel" correctly takes singular "requires."
**E) A number of interns was assigned to the summer festival.**

"A number of interns" needs a plural verb because it means several interns. The written "was assigned" wrongly treats "number" as a singular head. Swap in "several interns" — if that feels plural, keep the plural verb.

That fails here — rewrite as "A number of interns were assigned to the summer festival."
tasks.solution_overview:
Match briefing, planting plans, neighbour objections, parcel labelling, and festival interns — most lines here are already correct. Use the contrast with the one broken "a number of" item to lock the rule in.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Neither…nor proximity, together with inserts, there are, every, and a number of all appear in clean or near-clean form. The only intentional error sits on "a number of interns" with a singular verb. Everything else rewards careful subject-finding rather than hunt-for-typos guesswork.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm each head subject, ignore parenthetical with-phrases, and match there-constructions to the delayed noun. Save special attention for the final a-number-of line, where the singular "was" is the giveaway mismatch.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of open tickets is still above the club's service target.
Neither the solicitor nor the witnesses was available for the hearing.
There remain several chores that the housemates must finish.
The drama teacher, as well as the stage managers, are reviewing cues.
Each of the hiking clubs files its own risk assessment.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of open tickets is still above the club's service target.**

Singular "the number" correctly pairs with "is still above." Focus on "number," not plural "tickets," when you choose the verb. One count of open tickets stays singular even when that count is high.

Hold this: one "number" of open tickets correctly takes singular "is."
**B) Neither the solicitor nor the witnesses was available for the hearing.**

The nearer subject after neither…nor is plural "witnesses." The written "was available" wrongly follows singular "solicitor" at the front. Proximity overrides the first noun every time in this construction.

Reject this; the clean version is "Neither the solicitor nor the witnesses were available for the hearing."
**C) There remain several chores that the housemates must finish.**

Inverted "there remain" correctly agrees with plural "chores." There-constructions can use verbs other than be; you still match the following subject. Mentally flip it to "several chores remain" and the plural is obvious.

**Tip:** There + plural subject → plural verb, even with remain.

That works — plural "chores" correctly govern inverted "there remain."
**D) The drama teacher, as well as the stage managers, are reviewing cues.**

"As well as the stage managers" is parenthetical; the subject is singular "drama teacher." Managers in the insert are not co-subjects and must not pluralise the verb. Strip the as-well-as phrase before you choose the verb.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The drama teacher, as well as the stage managers, is reviewing cues."
**E) Each of the hiking clubs files its own risk assessment.**

"Each of the hiking clubs" takes singular "files." "Of the hiking clubs" is a prepositional phrase, not the subject head. "Each" still points to one club at a time for agreement.

Accept the line: "each of the hiking clubs" keeps singular "files."
tasks.solution_overview:
Service tickets, a hearing, housemate chores, stage cues, and hiking clubs raise the difficulty a notch. Two lines break agreement; three are clean models.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

You still need the number versus proximity after neither…nor, but now "there remain" and "as well as" join the cast. Inverted there-lines can use verbs other than be, yet agreement still tracks the following subject. As-well-as inserts remain parenthetical and must not pluralise a singular head.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the grammatical subject, mentally delete inserts, and match number — including with remain/appear after there. For each of, remember that the of-phrase is not the subject head.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of cyclists have demanded safer bike lanes.
Neither the understudy nor the chorus members were ready to rehearse.
The head gardener, along with her deputies, was copied on the schedule.
There is little room for another suitcase under the bunk.
The data on rainfall totals indicate a wetter spring.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A number of cyclists have demanded safer bike lanes.**

The plural sense of "a number of cyclists" calls for "have demanded." In exam English, "a number of" almost always takes a plural verb. Safer bike lanes is just the content; agreement rides on cyclists as a group.

Go with this: "a number of cyclists" correctly takes plural "have demanded."
**B) Neither the understudy nor the chorus members were ready to rehearse.**

Nearer plural "chorus members" correctly takes "were ready." Trust the last noun after nor and ignore singular "understudy" for agreement. Proximity is the whole rule in this construction.

This is sound — nearer plural "chorus members" rightly take "were ready."
**C) The head gardener, along with her deputies, was copied on the schedule.**

Head subject "head gardener" stays singular despite "along with her deputies," so "was copied" is right. Commas around the insert are a clue that it is not part of a compound subject. Deputies in the aside never pluralise the verb.

Call this correct: parenthetical deputies leave singular "was copied" intact.
**D) There is little room for another suitcase under the bunk.**

Uncountable "room" is singular, so "there is" fits. After there is/are, uncountables take singular even when "little" softens the quantity. Another suitcase does not make the subject plural.

**Tip:** Uncountable after there → there is.

Trust it: uncountable "room" after there correctly takes "there is."
**E) The data on rainfall totals indicate a wetter spring.**

Formal plural "data" correctly takes "indicate." Prefer plural agreement with data in formal writing and exam answers. Rainfall totals in the of-phrase do not turn data singular.

**Tip:** Formal data → plural verb.

Accept the line — formal plural "data" correctly takes "indicate."
tasks.solution_overview:
All five sentences in this bike-lane, rehearsal, gardening, bunk-bed, and rainfall set are grammatically sound. Treat them as clean reference models before the messier mixes return.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

You get textbook forms of a number of, neither…nor, along with, there is with an uncountable, and formal plural data. Nothing here is broken — the skill is recognising why each verb is already right. Uncountable "room" is the quiet singular after there.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm the head subject on every line and notice how each construction behaves when it is done correctly. Save these patterns: plural after a number of, proximity after nor, singular head despite along with, singular there is with uncountables, plural data.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Every member of the book club has cast a vote.
The number of broken toys have doubled year on year.
Neither the tenant nor the landlords' agents is contesting the clause.
There are a clear timeline attached to the renovation steps.
The captain, together with the non-playing coaches, intends to resign if the bid fails.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Every member of the book club has cast a vote.**

"Every member" takes singular "has cast." The of-phrase "of the book club" does not pluralise every/each. One member at a time is the agreement picture, even when the whole club votes.

That works: "every member" correctly takes singular "has cast."
**B) The number of broken toys have doubled year on year.**

"The number of broken toys" is one count, so the verb must be singular. The written "have doubled" wrongly agrees with "toys." Year-on-year growth does not change the subject's number.

Strike this and write "The number of broken toys has doubled year on year."
**C) Neither the tenant nor the landlords' agents is contesting the clause.**

The nearer subject after neither…nor is plural "agents." Possessive markers such as "landlords'" do not change that plural status. The written "is contesting" mismatches the nearer noun.

That nearer-noun miss fails — prefer "Neither the tenant nor the landlords' agents are contesting the clause."
**D) There are a clear timeline attached to the renovation steps.**

The real subject after there is singular "a clear timeline." Articles and adjectives often hide a singular head behind a plural of-phrase. Renovation steps are not the subject, so "there are" is wrong.

Mark it wrong and prefer "There is a clear timeline attached to the renovation steps."
**E) The captain, together with the non-playing coaches, intends to resign if the bid fails.**

Singular captain remains the subject; "intends" is correct despite "together with the non-playing coaches." Together with never creates a plural compound subject. Coaches in the insert stay outside the verb's agreement.

Singular head stays put — captain with a together-with aside still takes "intends."
tasks.solution_overview:
Book-club votes, broken toys, lease agents, renovation timelines, and a captain's resignation create a mixed true/false set. Slow down — proximity and there-heads are easy to rush past.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Every, the number of, neither…nor, there is/are, and together with all appear. The false lines hinge on agreeing with the wrong noun: toys instead of number, a timeline wrongly given there are, and plural agents with is. Singular captain with together with is the clean insert model.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the subject aloud before you judge the verb. For neither…nor, check the nearer noun's number even when possessives decorate it; for there-lines, spot singular heads hidden behind articles and adjectives.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of bakers was late with their sourdough orders.
Neither the guide nor the hikers was notified of the trail closure.
There is several pages missing from the scrapbook.
Each of the campsites have its own fire pit.
The data from last month's surveys show a narrower spread.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A number of bakers was late with their sourdough orders.**

"A number of bakers" means several bakers, so the verb must be plural. The written "was late" wrongly treats "number" as a singular head. If "their" later in the sentence feels natural, the verb is almost certainly plural.

Reject this; rewrite as "A number of bakers were late with their sourdough orders."
**B) Neither the guide nor the hikers was notified of the trail closure.**

Nearer plural "hikers" controls the verb after neither…nor. Singular "guide" at the front cannot save a singular verb. The written "was notified" fails the proximity test.

Score it false and use "Neither the guide nor the hikers were notified of the trail closure."
**C) There is several pages missing from the scrapbook.**

Plural "pages" requires "there are," not "there is." "Several" is a strong plural cue after there. Missing pages do not become singular just because the scrapbook is one object.

That fails — prefer "There are several pages missing from the scrapbook."
**D) Each of the campsites have its own fire pit.**

"Each of" needs a singular verb even when campsites look plural. "Its" already signals singular; keep the verb singular too. Campsites in the of-phrase do not govern agreement.

Don't accept that; fix to "Each of the campsites has its own fire pit."
**E) The data from last month's surveys show a narrower spread.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "show." Match data with plural verbs in exam answers unless told otherwise. Last month's surveys modify data; they do not make it singular.

**Tip:** Formal data → plural.

This is sound — formal plural "data" correctly takes "show."
tasks.solution_overview:
Sourdough orders, trail closures, a scrapbook, campsite fire pits, and survey spreads — four clear agreement errors surround one correct formal-data line.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A number of, neither…nor, there is/are, and each are all broken in familiar ways; only plural data with "show" is clean. Pronoun cues like "their" and "its" can confirm whether you are in plural or singular territory. Use those signals when the verb looks doubtful.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for the usual suspects before you mark true. Repair each false line by naming the real subject and rewriting the verb; keep formal plural data as your exam default on the last line.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the secretary nor the volunteers have released the minutes.
The project lead, along with the helpers, has signed the rota.
There remain two conditions before we can start the trek.
Every one of the shortlisted bakers meets the hygiene checklist.
The number of active memberships are being reduced this quarter.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the secretary nor the volunteers have released the minutes.**

Nearer plural "volunteers" correctly takes "have released." Read only from "nor" to the verb if the front of the sentence feels busy. Secretary at the start does not control agreement.

Accept the line: nearer plural "volunteers" correctly take "have released."
**B) The project lead, along with the helpers, has signed the rota.**

Singular project lead plus along with helpers correctly takes "has signed." Parenthetical helpers do not join the subject. Strip the insert and "the project lead has signed" must stand alone.

**Tip:** Along with ≠ and.

Hold onto this — singular "project lead" stays head with "has signed."
**C) There remain two conditions before we can start the trek.**

Plural "conditions" correctly takes "remain." Invert mentally: "two conditions remain before we can start." There-lines with remain still match the postponed plural subject.

The invert checks out: plural "conditions" correctly take "there remain."
**D) Every one of the shortlisted bakers meets the hygiene checklist.**

"Every one" is singular, so "meets" is right. "Every one of the shortlisted bakers" still points to a single unit for agreement. Hygiene checklist content does not change number.

That works: "every one of the … bakers" still takes singular "meets."
**E) The number of active memberships are being reduced this quarter.**

"The number of active memberships" is singular — one count being reduced. Passive voice does not change the number of the subject. The written "are being reduced" wrongly agrees with "memberships."

**Trap:** Agreeing with the of-phrase noun in a passive still looks polished — and still fails.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The number of active memberships is being reduced this quarter."
tasks.solution_overview:
Minutes, rotas, trek conditions, bakers on a shortlist, and membership tallies sit at mid-difficulty. Inserts, every one of, and passive voice appear — agreement rules do not change.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Neither…nor, along with, there remain, every one of, and the number of (with a wrong plural passive) are the toolkit. Passive voice is the soft distractor: "are being reduced" still has to match a singular number. Every one of remains singular despite a plural of-phrase.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep the same subject-finding habit and do not let construction noise distract you. Mentally delete along-with inserts and asides after there; for passives, still ask what the subject is before you accept the auxiliary's number.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the driver nor the passengers was listed on the boarding sheet.
A number of rules in the house agreement has been waived.
There is too many variables still open in the recipe.
The chair, as well as the committee secretaries, was delayed by the vote.
The data collected overnight do not yet justify a schedule change.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the driver nor the passengers was listed on the boarding sheet.**

Nearer plural "passengers" needs a plural verb after neither…nor. Long titles after nor still keep their plural number. Driver at the front is irrelevant to the verb choice.

**Trap:** A singular opener after neither…nor often fools you into writing was — proximity still rules.

That proximity error fails — rewrite as "Neither the driver nor the passengers were listed on the boarding sheet."
**B) A number of rules in the house agreement has been waived.**

"A number of rules" needs a plural verb because several rules have been waived. The of-phrase noun is plural, and "a number of" takes that plurality. House-agreement wording does not singularise the group.

**Trap:** Perfect passive "has been waived" still looks careful while disagreeing with a plural group.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "A number of rules in the house agreement have been waived."
**C) There is too many variables still open in the recipe.**

"Too many variables" is plural, so write "there are," not "there is." "Many" after there is a strong plural signal. Open variables in the recipe stay plural.

**Tip:** Many / several / few after there → plural verb.

Score it false and use "There are too many variables still open in the recipe."
**D) The chair, as well as the committee secretaries, was delayed by the vote.**

Singular "chair" governs "was delayed"; secretaries are only an as-well-as insert. Cross out the insert and re-read: "the chair was delayed by the vote." The insert never becomes a co-subject.

Call this correct: singular "chair" with an as-well-as aside takes "was delayed."
**E) The data collected overnight do not yet justify a schedule change.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "do not yet justify." Past participles after data ("collected overnight") do not make the noun singular. Keep the plural exam default.

Trust the exam default: formal plural "data" correctly takes "do not."
tasks.solution_overview:
Boarding sheets, house rules, recipe variables, a delayed chair, and overnight data hide their subjects inside longer noun phrases. Peel each sentence to its skeleton before you accept the verb.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Neither…nor, a number of, there is/are, as well as, and formal plural data recur with denser modifiers. False singulars after plural nearer nouns and after "too many" are the main failures. The clean as-well-as line shows a singular chair surviving a plural insert.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Strip relative clauses and inserts, then apply the familiar tests. Quantity words like many after there almost always demand a plural verb; data with past participial modifiers still stays formally plural.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Each monthly playlist submitted by the DJs goes to the host first.
Neither the landlord nor the tenants' solicitors have consented to the repair plan.
There appears to be several gaps in the packing checklist.
The podcast host, together with two editors, are pitching tomorrow.
The number of unsettled bookings has dropped below fifty.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Each monthly playlist submitted by the DJs goes to the host first.**

"Each monthly playlist" takes singular "goes." Long modifiers after each do not change singularity. Submitted-by-the-DJs material is descriptive only.

Right call: "each … playlist" correctly takes singular "goes."
**B) Neither the landlord nor the tenants' solicitors have consented to the repair plan.**

Nearer plural "solicitors" correctly takes "have consented." Possessive "tenants'" does not make the nearer noun singular. Repair-plan content is irrelevant to agreement.

Accept the line — nearer plural "solicitors" rightly take "have consented."
**C) There appears to be several gaps in the packing checklist.**

Although "appears" can introduce a clause, the logical subject "several gaps" is plural. In there + appear/seem, still match the notional plural subject in careful exam English. Formal tone does not excuse a number clash.

**Trap:** "There appears to be several" sounds careful but still disagrees with a plural complement.

That verb number fails — prefer "There appear to be several gaps in the packing checklist."
**D) The podcast host, together with two editors, are pitching tomorrow.**

Singular host plus together with two editors needs a singular verb. Editors after together with are not co-subjects. Pitching tomorrow does not change the head subject's number.

**Trap:** Together with two editors looks like a compound subject — it is only an insert.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The podcast host, together with two editors, is pitching tomorrow."
**E) The number of unsettled bookings has dropped below fifty.**
